title: Ash, Lime, and the Tired Soil

pages.text: For four years in a row, the JHS school farm had grown only maize. This term the rains were steady, and the class had added plenty of sulphate of ammonia fertiliser. Still, the young maize leaves turned pale yellow-green with purplish edges, and the stalks stayed thin. Yaw sighed beside the fence. “Let us clear the bush behind the football field, burn it, and start a fresh farm. The ash will feed the crops.” Akua shook her head. “Before we burn any bush, let us find out why this soil is tired.”
sentences: For four years in a row, the JHS school farm had grown only maize.
This term the rains were steady, and the class had added plenty of sulphate of ammonia fertiliser.
Still, the young maize leaves turned pale yellow-green with purplish edges, and the stalks stayed thin.
Yaw sighed beside the fence.
“Let us clear the bush behind the football field, burn it, and start a fresh farm.
The ash will feed the crops.” Akua shook her head.
“Before we burn any bush, let us find out why this soil is tired.”
pages.alt: Three JHS students in uniform and boots standing beside a plot of stunted, yellowish-leaved maize plants, holding notebooks thoughtfully.

pages.text: Madam Agyeiwaa, the District Agricultural Extension Officer, showed the class a simple test. They took soil from three spots on the plot, stirred each sample into distilled water, and let the soil settle. Then they dipped test papers into the liquid. Blue litmus paper turned red. The universal indicator matched 4.8 on the pH scale, which is strongly acidic. “Most crops prefer soil that is only slightly acidic or nearly neutral,” Madam Agyeiwaa explained. “Heavy rain washes calcium and magnesium down out of reach of the roots. Using a lot of ammonium fertiliser year after year also makes soil more acidic. In acidic soil, roots struggle to take up nutrients such as phosphorus.”

pages.alt: Close-up gouache scene at a wooden garden bench showing clear jars of settled soil and water, blue litmus paper turning red, and a colour pH chart pointing to pH 4.8.

pages.text: “Shall we add more fertiliser to force the maize to grow?” Yaw asked. “No. That would make the soil more acidic and waste money,” Madam Agyeiwaa replied. “When an acid meets a base, they react. We call this neutralisation. Agricultural lime contains calcium carbonate, a base, so it reduces soil acidity. But test first, then apply only the amount an extension officer advises. And never mix lime directly with ammonium fertiliser. They can react and release ammonia gas, so the nitrogen escapes into the air. Wood ash is also a base, Yaw, but nobody can measure its strength by eye. It is no substitute for tested lime.”

Wood ash is also a base, Yaw, but nobody can measure its strength by eye.
It is no substitute for tested lime.”
pages.alt: Madam Agyeiwaa drawing a clear chalkboard equation of neutralisation beside bags labelled Agricultural Lime and Compost, with a warning cross over mixing lime directly with ammonium fertiliser.

pages.text: Next, Rashida gently dug up a healthy cowpea plant from the border bed. Tiny round swellings dotted its roots. “Root nodules,” she said, smiling. “My father showed me these on our farm. Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut, and soya bean keep helpful bacteria called Rhizobium inside them.” Madam Agyeiwaa nodded. “Those bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air in the soil and change it into a form the plant can use to make proteins. This is nitrogen fixation. Grow a legume after maize, leave its roots and leaves in the soil, and the soil slowly becomes richer. Crop rotation also breaks the life cycle of some pests.”

pages.text: That week, Social Studies and RME turned to bush burning. Burning gives the soil one quick dose of ash. But repeated burning destroys the organic matter in the soil and kills earthworms and other useful organisms. It leaves the topsoil bare, so rain washes it away. A fire can also escape and destroy a neighbour’s cocoa farm. “Our elders say the land belongs to the ancestors, the living, and those not yet born,” Yaw said slowly. Rashida added, “Christian and Islamic teaching both warn against wasteful destruction. If we hand tired, eroded soil to the next class, we have broken their trust.”

pages.alt: Split educational illustration contrasting dark, earthworm-rich mulched soil holding moisture on the left against cracked, scorched, eroding bare soil after bush burning on the right.

pages.text: Guided by Madam Agyeiwaa, the students ran a fair test. They spread the advised amount of agricultural lime on half of the plot before planting and left the other half untreated for comparison. They tried mulching too, covering the beds with dry grass to hold moisture and add humus as it rotted. Then they planned a four-bed crop rotation: maize, cowpea, tomatoes, and cassava. By the end of term, the cowpea was thriving, and the maize on the limed half looked greener than the rest. The class recorded every change. “Testing the soil gave us a better answer than burning more land,” Akua said. Yaw grinned. “And it cost us no bush.”

Yaw grinned.

activities.question: Blue litmus paper turned red and the indicator showed pH 4.8. What did this reveal about the soil in the maize plot?
options: The soil contained pure distilled water with zero minerals
The soil was strongly alkaline with pH above 9.0
The soil was strongly acidic, preventing the maize from absorbing nutrients

activities.question: Why should farmers NOT mix lime (a base) directly with ammonium fertiliser?
options: Lime turns ammonium fertiliser into solid granite rock instantly
They can react and release ammonia gas, so valuable nitrogen is lost to the air
Calcium carbonate kills Rhizobium bacteria from five kilometres away

activities.question: How do leguminous crops such as cowpea and groundnut naturally enrich exhausted farm soil?
options: Bacteria in their root nodules convert nitrogen gas into plant nutrients
Their leaves drip hydrochloric acid onto weeds during the night
They remove all organic humus and earthworms from topsoil

activities.question: Apply it: A farmer notices yellow maize leaves. What should the farmer do before adding more fertiliser?
options: Add extra fertiliser immediately without checking the soil
Test the soil and ask an agricultural extension officer for advice
Burn the entire field to make the soil look clean

activities.prompt: Put the steps for restoring the tired soil in the correct order.
items: Test the soil with an indicator to discover that it is strongly acidic.
Apply the recommended amount of agricultural lime before planting.
Rotate maize with nitrogen-fixing cowpeas and protect soil with mulch.
Record how the crops respond and compare the limed and untreated halves.

activities.definition: A reaction between an acid and a base that reduces acidity or alkalinity. The products depend on the substances used.
distractors: The washing away of fertile topsoil by heavy rainwater runoff
The burning of dry weeds to clear farmland before the rainy season

glossary.definition: A numerical scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic (below 7), neutral (7), or alkaline/basic (above 7) a substance is.
A reaction between an acid and a base. With some bases, such as carbonates, carbon dioxide is also released.
The conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia by certain bacteria, including those living in the root nodules of legumes.
Growing different types of crops in a planned sequence on the same land across seasons.
Covering topsoil around plants with dry leaves, straw, or grass clippings to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, prevent erosion, and add humus as it decays.
